quote: “So,” I said incredulously, “if God exists or doesn’t exist, that has absolutely no effect on how it would be good for people to think or act? I think even a rabbi would look a little askance at that.”
content: Kaplan's Reconstructionism is real, but the woman described herself as Orthodox and "vigorously defended the assertion that she believed in God." An Orthodox rabbi works under Maimonides' Thirteen Principles, the first of which is the existence of God. Their verse form, Yigdal, is sung in the Orthodox liturgy, and Maimonides rules the denier a heretic (Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:7). The Yerushalmi line Fable quotes also continues: keep My Torah, "for the light within it will bring them back to good" (Lamentations Rabbah has "back to Me"). Practice is valued there because it leads back to God. That is the opposite of indifference to whether God exists. A rabbi of her movement would have looked askance, as the essay predicted.

quote: you get the same sort of placebo benefit that would actually come from a successful self-deception
content: Lim and Putnam support the essay here. If the measured benefits of religion flow through the congregation and not through private belief (Lim & Putnam 2010), then the woman's theory, that she benefits from believing things she does not believe, is false about where the benefits come from, which is the essay's diagnosis. The essay is not trying to take away anyone's Purim or synagogue friendships. It targets one specific belief: that self-deception pays and that she has managed it. The placebo is offered as an explanation of why that belief persists, not of the attendance effect. A person who knew the benefits were social could keep the community and drop the belief in belief, which is what the essay is arguing for.

quote: This is why intelligent people only have a certain amount of time (measured in subjective time spent thinking about religion) to become atheists.
content: The switching data describe a window. Pew's study of religious change found that most Americans who leave the faith of their childhood do so before age 24, and that most of those who leave and later return also do so early (Pew Research Center, Faith in Flux, 2009, no DOI). A religious identity that has survived into middle age is far less likely to change, which is the pattern of a deadline. Fable's dilemma also misreads the essay's variable. The clock runs on time spent "thinking about and defending your religion," which is practice at motivated reasoning. The sequence says that practice entrenches (Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People) and that other practice corrects. The same distinction is in the data: myside bias does not fall as intelligence rises (Stanovich & West 2007).
